item.title: How Islamophobia Moved From the Fringe to the Mainstream in Texas
item.description:
Ghulam Kehar rose before dawn in early June to attend the day’s first prayer at his local mosque in Irving, Texas, before heading off for a monthslong deployment with the U.S. Coast Guard.

He had been deployed before, but this time was different. He felt apprehensive about leaving his wife and four children behind in Texas, even for a short while.

Rhetorical attacks on Muslims by top Texas leaders had become more pronounced, and seemed to be trickling down. At his mosque, the Valley Ranch Islamic Center, and others across the state, congregants and religious leaders swapped stories of ugly comments directed at them while praying in public or sitting in public parks.

In recent months, a man was arrested and charged with making a terroristic threat at a major new Islamic center in Houston. Not far away, in Conroe, a woman told Muslim shoppers at a grocery store they were “not welcome in this state or this country” — after losing her job, she received nearly $250,000 from supporters after video of her comments circulated widely. In McKinney, a Dallas suburb, a woman grabbed a former mayor and stuffed paper with an anti-Muslim message down his shirt during a heated City Council hearing over a mosque expansion.

“Leaving them alone in this environment, it would be a little worrisome,” Mr. Kehar said of his family. “It’s just the fear of what’s being spewed out there.”

He arranged for his family to join him on his deployment near the Canadian border as soon as they could get there.

Mr. Kehar, who grew up in California, is part of a growing number of Muslims who moved to Texas in recent decades in search of good schools, affordable homes and a thriving community of fellow believers. The Dallas-Fort Worth area has been a particularly strong magnet for families like his. Dozens of mosques have opened. Some are expanding. Others, like the glittering DeSoto House of Peace, south of Dallas, aim to provide new anchors for Muslim communities in Texas.

“This is the place to be for American Muslims,” said Tammam Alwan, who moved to Irving from Detroit after discovering the community through religious videos online. “I made a prayer: Please, God, send me to Irving.”

But as the communities have grown, so has the resentment against Muslims.

The promise to combat “radical Islam” has long been a part of Republican politics. The rhetoric has only intensified nationally, as Muslims like Zohran Mamdani, the democratic socialist mayor of New York City, and Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, won major races.

But politicians in Texas have gone beyond words, turning the power of the state against some Muslim groups.

A major turning point arrived in early 2025, after members of the East Plano Islamic Center unveiled plans for a real estate development centered on a new mosque in farmland east of Dallas. The opposition was immediate and intense.

State leaders, including Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton, have since opened investigations into Muslim institutions across Texas. They’ve sought to block the real estate development and investigate religious divorce counseling. Mr. Abbott threatened to take state funding from Texas airports that provide ritual washing stations for Muslim travelers, ordered the cancellation of a private water park party celebrating a Muslim holiday and labeled the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a national civil rights group, as a terrorist group — a step that even the Trump administration has so far not taken. (Florida followed Texas in applying the same label to CAIR.)

Efforts by Republican state leaders to restrict Islamic practice have coincided with a push to expand Christianity’s place in public life. In June, Texas became the first state to mandate Bible readings in public schools, where lawmakers had already required prayer time and the posting of the Ten Commandments.

For many conservative voters in Texas, Islam has replaced the border as a major concern since early last year, Republican consultants have said. Anti-Muslim activists and hard-right candidates have increasingly described Islam as incompatible with American values. They warn that the United States could soon look like Europe, where Muslim populations are larger.

“I won’t rest until every Muslim is gone,” one statewide Republican candidate, Bo French, wrote on social media this summer.

Muslim leaders in Texas have debated how to respond. Some counseled outreach. Others were frustrated with the return of rhetoric that had been largely dormant since the 9/11 attacks despite years of trying to foster interfaith understanding.

“We’ve constantly tried to point to our record and hope that our record will organically speak for itself,” Dr. Omar Suleiman, a prominent Muslim scholar, said in an interview at the Valley Ranch mosque. “We tried that, and it did nothing for us.”

The moment called for a posture of “strength,” Mr. Suleiman said, and a robust legal defense against what he said were false attacks. “We have to actually make lying legally and politically costly to these people,” he said. “We have to fight them back.”

He pointed to the religious protections afforded by the U.S. Constitution as the basis for such a defense. But recently, hard-line conservatives have been looking for a way to deny those protections.

In what would be an apparent first, one avenue being explored in Texas is to try to use state law to ban or regulate some Islamic cultural practices, such tribunals for marriage and other decisions governed by religious rules, often referred to as Shariah law.

Some want to do it as soon as the Texas Legislature meets next year.

“One of the first things we’re going to try to do is define what a religion is,” said State Representative Alan Schoolcraft, a San Antonio Republican. “Islam itself is not just a religion. It’s much more than a religion.”

Texas’ Muslim population remains small, around 1 or 2 percent of all residents. Precise figures are hard to come by, because the census does not ask about religion, but surveys by the Pew Research Center, and estimates by state officials, put the population between 300,000 and 500,000 people. Among the most populous states, only New York and Illinois have a higher share of Muslims than Texas.

The Dallas-Fort Worth area has been a popular destination. In recent years, one of its growing communities is in Irving around the Valley Ranch Islamic Center, the city’s second mosque. Founded in 2009, the mosque has a large campus and is planning a 31,000-square-foot expansion, with a cafe and basketball court. At a recent nightly prayer, families struggled to find parking.

“We’re growing faster than expected,” said Sheikh Yaser Birjas, who has led the congregation since 2010.

Mr. Birjas said the mosque’s success was in part thanks to its early embrace of technology. New people discovered its services online. Some moved to Texas to join.

One indication of the growing community comes from census data on international migration from Muslim-majority countries to the United States. That population grew in the Dallas-Fort Worth metro area to more than 159,000 in 2024, from about 79,000 people a decade earlier — growing five times faster than the population as a whole.

Another indication can be found in the increasing number of Muslim congregations.

In the four biggest Dallas-Fort Worth counties, the number of mosques nearly tripled to 76 by 2020, up from 28 two decades earlier, according to data from the Association of Religion Data Archives. In Collin County, a fast-growing suburban area north of Dallas, the number quadrupled, to 12 from three.

The increase was notable, but the number of mosques remains small. By comparison, the four counties have more than 3,000 evangelical Christian congregations.

Nearly every speech at the Texas State Republican Convention in June included some expression of anti-Muslim sentiment. Multiple conference panels warned of a Muslim invasion. Combating Shariah law — the Islamic code that guides the observant — was named a top legislative priority.

In the convention hall, the Texas House’s new Sharia-Free Caucus had a booth. Amy Mekelburg, a prominent anti-Muslim influencer, presented a video warning that Texas barbecue restaurants were being replaced by “Arab shopping plazas” — part of a coordinated “takeover.”

The focus on Muslims gained new traction with President Trump’s first White House run. In 2015, the mayor of Irving, Beth Van Duyne gained national attention by railing against Shariah law. (She is now a member of Congress.) Two years later, Texas Republicans passed anti-Shariah legislation as part of a wave of bills pushed by the Center for Security Policy, a hard-right Washington think tank.

For a time, the party moved away from Islam to concentrate on immigration, the pandemic and gender politics.

But some on the far right began focusing on a different and more contentious message: that Islam is not a religion but a political ideology.

Then came the proposed real estate development with a mosque outside Dallas, known at the time as EPIC City. “This is how the West falls,” Ms. Mekelburg wrote on social media in February 2025.

Her rhetoric caught Mr. Abbott’s attention, and he soon initiated state investigations into the proposed development and the mosque community, the East Plano Islamic Center, or EPIC, that supported it.

Anthony Holm, a Republican political consultant, said concerns about Islam were an extension of Republican voters’ fears about illegal immigration — and help explain Mr. Abbott’s focus. “Anything he does is poll-driven,” Mr. Holm said of the governor.

Mr. Abbott has used his terror designation of CAIR to try to restrict other Islamic groups. The council is challenging the designation in court.

“We experience waves of Islamophobia,” said Shaimaa Zayan of CAIR’s Austin chapter. “This is the worst wave.”

About 300 people gathered at a Dallas movie theater in late May to watch a documentary film billed as revealing “the disastrous effect of Islam in America.”

The event’s sponsors included a nearby Christian ministry, a group of Jewish conservatives, several Republican women’s groups and two local county Republican parties.

“Most of the people that are speaking up are Christian,” Frank X. Panico, the film’s director, who is Catholic, said as he mingled by the popcorn machines.

As the Muslim population has grown in Texas, an assertive Christianity has also taken root. Hard-line conservative Christians characterize the situation not as a demographic shift, but as a spiritual battle.

The documentary, “The Great American Conflict,” contained a mix of theological, political and cultural warnings. It depicted Islam as a force that could pull communities to the left — citing Mayor Mamdani of New York — and also threaten women’s freedom.

The audience heard Texas was at the center of this cultural struggle.

“This is the battlefield right now,” Erick Stakelbeck, a host on the Trinity Broadcasting Network, said at the event.

Barbara Isaacs, an activist in Collin County, distributed a pamphlet encouraging Texans to get involved with their local governments to prevent or slow the construction of mosques.

“Share this with your friends, your church members,” she urged the crowd.

Farhat Shaikh, a doctor living in Frisco, north of Dallas, stood outside a polling place during a sharply contested mayoral runoff election in June.

For many on the hard right, Frisco — with its large South Asian and Muslim populations — was the epicenter of the fight for Texas’ future.

Dr. Shaikh urged voters to support Mark Hill, a former school board trustee, who vowed to unite the city. Mr. Hill’s opponent, Rod Vilhauer, talked about the need for Muslims to assimilate into American culture, and some of his supporters warned of a Muslim “takeover.”

Mr. Hill prevailed in the election. Still, for Dr. Shaikh, the divisive campaign put Muslims like her in a kind of bind.

Assimilation means joining institutions and being “part of the decision making,” she said. “I’m part of the P.T.A., I volunteer for my community, I’m a practicing physician. I am assimilating.” But being active can also be attacked as trying to “take over,” she said.

The question of assimilation has animated Texas legislators like Mr. Schoolcraft, and fueled calls for a definition of religion in Texas law. Mr. Schoolcraft hoped such legislation would encourage Muslims to more fully assimilate and not create enclaves, such as the EPIC City development.

“I’m not saying totally abandon your culture,” Mr. Schoolcraft said. “But try to become a citizen where you’re living. Otherwise there’s going to be conflict.”

Texas Republicans have warned of Muslims seeking to create a parallel justice system. Some pointed to a small decade-old organization based in Dallas, the Islamic Tribunal, which provides religious consultation to women seeking divorce, including in abusive marriages. Mr. Paxton began an investigation.

A lawyer for the organization said its religious guidance — like that of a Jewish rabbinical court or a Catholic tribunal — was protected by the First Amendment.

“We are not a court,” said Taher El-Badawi, who founded the Islamic Tribunal.

Recasting Islam as a political ideology would be unprecedented as a legislative strategy, said Asma T. Uddin, a religious liberty lawyer, and “a way of winning the religious liberty fight before it starts, by defining the other side out of the category.”

American courts have avoided defining religion over the years. In 2010, Tennessee residents tried to stop a new mosque, arguing it was not entitled to be treated as a house of worship because Islam was not a religion.

The Justice Department responded in a brief that “Islam is plainly a religion” protected by the First Amendment. Whether the department under Mr. Trump would take the same position was an open question.

For now, local Muslim institutions have defended themselves on constitutional and legal grounds, and promised to continue their work.

“The Muslim community is a huge community in Dallas and they need help,” said Mr. El-Badawi of the Islamic Tribunal. “We are religious help. That’s all.”

Edgar Sandoval contributed reporting from San Antonio, Sasha von Oldershausen from Austin and Jeff Adelson from New York.

item.title: How Louisiana’s New Surgeon General Wants to Transform Public Health
item.description:
Dr. Evelyn Griffin had led a life out of the spotlight until she testified at the Louisiana statehouse five years ago and experienced what she called her “great awakening.”

The state health department wanted to add Covid vaccines to the school immunization schedule, a move no state has ever implemented. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., then known as a leading vaccine skeptic, had already claimed the Covid shot was “the deadliest vaccine ever made” during a poster board presentation at the legislative hearing.

Dr. Griffin, a longtime obstetrician, relied on nearly identical images during her own blistering testimony against the proposal. After the hearing, she expected splashy headlines about Mr. Kennedy’s assertions, shifting the public debate over Covid policies and vaccines. But that did not happen; one news outlet dismissed him as a promulgator of propaganda. Dr. Griffin was shocked.

That is “when I saw how the world worked,” she recalled in a podcast interview. Dr. Griffin said she and her husband, a vascular surgeon, decided to take action and “shine light on things.”

Now, Mr. Kennedy is the nation’s health secretary, and Dr. Griffin holds prominent roles that position her to help carry out his vision.

Last September, Mr. Kennedy appointed her to the advisory panel for federal immunization policy, where she voted to recommend limiting access to Covid vaccines and ending universal newborn immunizations for hepatitis B, steps that a federal judge has blocked. In December, Gov. Jeff Landry of Louisiana, a conservative Republican and ally of President Trump, named Dr. Griffin as the state’s surgeon general.

That makes her the top public health physician in Louisiana, which has the worst health outcomes in the nation.

She is an unconventional choice. Dr. Griffin has no background or specialty training in infectious disease or public health. She is aligned with alternative health movements — including Make American Healthy Again, or MAHA — and has hosted some speakers promoting fringe medical views.

Dr. Griffin declined interview requests for this article. “My vision as Louisiana’s surgeon general is to help shift our health care system toward preventing disease, not just managing or treating it,” she said in a statement.

Eight months into her tenure, she has yet to make major changes at the health department. She has faced hurdles in her efforts to tighten access to vaccines and limit public health powers, testifying on several bills that legislators rejected.

Still, Dr. Griffin’s political rise reflects the gains of Mr. Kennedy’s vaccine agenda at the state level, a vital testing ground for laws aimed at eroding government mandates. State officials have enormous power to set health policy and beat back infectious disease outbreaks. While Dr. Griffin’s post is largely a bully pulpit, she could spur real change by advising the governor, state health secretary and lawmakers.

Some public health and infectious disease experts warned that if Dr. Griffin eventually succeeded in curtailing the state’s authority, illnesses and deaths could escalate and Louisiana could be hamstrung in a future pandemic. At one vaccine panel meeting last year, she said it was “unclear” whether vaccines were linked to autism, as Mr. Kennedy has suggested. When asked by The New York Times, she declined to say whether she believed any vaccines should be mandated for schoolchildren.

“Someone who has expressed the views she has, who’s now in a public policy position, is very dangerous,” said Dr. Georges C. Benjamin, the chief executive of the American Public Health Association.

But Dr. Kirk Milhoan, a pastor and pediatric cardiologist who serves as chairman of the federal vaccine panel, defended Dr. Griffin as an “excellent choice” for surgeon general. “No one should be afraid of Dr. Evelyn Griffin having the heart’s desire to take care of the population of Louisiana,” he said in an interview.

While Dr. Griffin is on a learning curve as a political novice, she has signaled big ambitions.

She called for “dramatic transformational change” during a public meeting in January, promising to focus on women’s health, rural health and the root causes of disease. An accompanying slide presentation said Louisiana would lead through “family, faith, and fearlessness.”

Dr. Griffin, 49, often cites her family background in explaining her trajectory.

She was born Ewelina Bulczynski under Communist rule in Poland in 1976. When she was 5 years old, her family defected to a refugee camp in Austria before immigrating to Canada. She and her two brothers later came to the United States to practice as physicians. She has credited this history with giving her a “different perspective” as a doctor and influencing her skepticism of government mandates."My parents escaped Communist Poland so that we could come here for the freedoms, such as medical freedom, that this country has,” she told Louisiana lawmakers in 2022.

She met her husband, Joseph Griffin, while they attended Ross University School of Medicine in Dominica. After residency programs in New Orleans, they settled in Baton Rouge and raised two children.

People who have known Dr. Griffin during her 20-year career delivering babies and treating women described her as a kind, caring and smart physician. “Patients loved her,” said Dr. Francis Dauterive, who worked with her.

In the years before the pandemic, Dr. Griffin had noticed a rise in chronic health problems among her patients. She began studying how nutrition and lifestyle choices could treat and prevent illness, and pursued online training in functional medicine. She started an Instagram account filled with images of jackfruit sloppy joes and vegan jambalaya, her dog lounging on a yoga mat, and her backyard strawberry plants.

She also learned of Barbara O’Neill, a Christian wellness figure popular on social media. Ms. O’Neill was barred in 2019 from giving medical advice in Australia after claiming that cancer was caused by a fungus and could be treated with baking soda, and that vaccines caused “an epidemic of ADHD, autism, epilepsy and cot death.” In a 2025 podcast, Dr. Griffin called Ms. O’Neill a “sage” teacher who was ostracized for focusing on lifestyle solutions to medical issues. She said she kept Ms. O’Neill’s advice for a healthy life — including exercise, sunshine and trust in God — posted on her fridge.

But it was the pandemic that transformed her career. In multiple speeches and interviews, she said she began to question public health guidance and that of her former employer, Ochsner Health, Louisiana’s largest health system, on masking, vaccines and mandates.

Dr. Griffin wanted to share research with colleagues that wasn’t “mainstream” science, as she put it, studies she said were from contacts in Europe on early Covid treatments. Dr. Griffin was repeatedly rebuffed, she said.

Eventually, she resigned. “I’m going to stick to my principles,” she later recalled thinking. She now works at the Baton Rouge General health system. Ochsner officials declined to comment.

Louisiana had been hit hard by the pandemic. By December 2021, more than 14,000 people had died from Covid. Earlier that summer, the Delta surge killed six pregnant women there in two months, and maternal health organizations were urging vaccination.

But in her testimony to lawmakers in December, Dr. Griffin had questioned the vaccine’s safety after health officials had reported rare adverse reactions. She invoked a public health catastrophe: The drug thalidomide, prescribed during pregnancy in Europe (and tested in the United States) in the 1950s, had left thousands of babies with missing or malformed limbs. She also reminded lawmakers of the Nuremberg trials, where Nazi collaborators had been sentenced to death for medical experimentation.

“So everyone has to be on notice when making these types of decisions,” Dr. Griffin said, looking at the politicians. The state later dropped plans to require Covid vaccines for students.

Dr. Griffin and her husband have since embedded themselves in Louisiana’s right-leaning alternative health communities. They have espoused views that, amid the swirl of social-media-fueled wellness trends, pandemic backlash and widespread dismay over Americans’ poor health, have become ascendant in the second Trump presidency.

Dr. Griffin returned to the State Capitol over the next three years to testify for favored causes, including bills supported by Health Freedom Louisiana, a group aligned with Mr. Kennedy. One would have expanded access to ivermectin, an antiparasitic drug popular among vaccine skeptics, though numerous studies have shown it is ineffective in treating Covid, and another would have banned future government health mandates, which Dr. Griffin has called “a slippery slope.” Neither got out of committee. She also testified in support of a ban on gender-transition treatments for minors, which became law.

After the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022 and Louisiana’s near-total abortion ban took effect, Dr. Griffin became an ally of Louisiana Right to Life, the state’s leading anti-abortion group. She recorded videos arguing the law did not impede pregnancy care. The ban was later found to delay miscarriage treatment and lead to unnecessary C-sections, according to doctors and reproductive rights groups.

Dr. Griffin and her husband struck up a friendship with Tony Spell, the pastor of Life Tabernacle Church in Baton Rouge, sometimes joining him for Bible study. Pastor Spell refused to shut his evangelical church during the pandemic, leading to criminal charges that were overturned by the Louisiana Supreme Court. Dr. Griffin called him “an absolute hero.”

She has spoken at annual health freedom gatherings on the church’s sprawling grounds, and launched her own wellness events there two years ago. Guests have talked about backyard gardening, naturopathic medicine, the benefits of doulas and raw milk — a passion of Mr. Kennedy’s — which recently sickened nearly a dozen Louisiana residents.

One speaker, an OB-GYN, said contraception encouraged abortion. Another, an ophthalmologist, questioned the safety of wireless technology, as has Dr. Griffin. Quoting Ms. O’Neill, the Australian wellness figure, Dr. Griffin warned the crowd to “stay away from sunscreen,” adding there were “lots and lots of chemicals” in it.

Spirituality is “the foundation for health,” she said during the event in 2025, and some of her speakers have presented faith in Jesus as essential to being healthy. At the 2024 gathering, Dr. Sean Troxclair, an internist who is now her deputy, said that when he was “injured” by a vaccine, “I got with Jesus.” He added, “if you’re not with him, no matter what you do, you’re not going to get better.”

In written comments to The Times, Dr. Griffin said that faith was not a prerequisite for good health, and that she “may not share every perspective presented” by her speakers.

Dr. Griffin’s appointment is among Governor Landry’s wider efforts to move Louisiana, already a deeply red state, further to the right. He’s supported a crackdown on doctors who mail abortion pills to Louisiana patients and a lawsuit against the Food and Drug Administration to stop the practice nationwide. The Supreme Court said the pills could still be sent by mail while the F.D.A. case continues in the lower courts.

The governor’s first appointee as surgeon general, Dr. Ralph Abraham, another supporter of Mr. Kennedy, blocked his staff from promoting any vaccines amid an outbreak of whooping cough that killed two babies.

Dr. Griffin has begun her tenure more quietly, seeking ties with the state’s medical community while trying to find her place in a health department hierarchy where the secretary still wields much of the power.

For her staff, she’s recruited figures from wellness and vaccine-skeptical circles, including Dr. Troxclair and Dr. Kathleen Willis, an internist who has questioned the safety of the childhood vaccine schedule, as has Mr. Trump.

A surprising presence in the department is Dr. Griffin’s husband, whom she’s called “like-minded.” Though he is not employed by the agency, he has joined her appointments with state and federal officials and participated in department meetings, sometimes providing feedback or asking questions, according to two people present at the sessions. Dr. Griffin has also placed him on a Medicaid advisory committee. Dr. Griffin said in a statement that he was “not involved in formal decision-making.”

Bruce D. Greenstein, the state health secretary, introduced the couple during a public meeting in January, saying, “We basically get two doctors for the price of one.” In May, Dr. Griffin’s husband joined the governor on a contentious trip to Greenland, which Mr. Trump has periodically threatened to control.

Dr. Griffin’s beliefs represent a shift away from public health policies that prioritize the protection of the wider community in favor of ones that prioritize individual choice. Like Mr. Kennedy, she has said this is necessary to restore faith in public health systems battered by the anger over pandemic restrictions.

Such a reframing of the government’s role would upend longstanding public health principles and risk harming society’s most vulnerable, said Dr. Paul A. Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

“Are we in no way responsible for people who we are going to sit next to on a bus or get into a crowded elevator?” he asked. “Do we have no sense of responsibility to other members of society?”

Florida’s former health secretary and surgeon general Dr. Scott Rivkees, whose successor tried to roll back vaccine mandates, said rising vaccine skepticism was already contributing to outbreaks of measles and whooping cough. “This is something that our country will regret as we start seeing our sons, daughters, neighbors, friends, cousins, pay the price,” he said in an interview.

Even though Dr. Griffin has allied herself with some lawmakers in the Republican-controlled Legislature, she testified on three bills this spring that failed to proceed. One would have created new vaccine informed-consent requirements — including banning mothers from agreeing to vaccines for 12 hours after giving birth, when Dr. Griffin said hormones and other factors could impede their thinking.

Another would have significantly limited the government’s ability to require vaccines, testing or masks in a future outbreak, mandates that Dr. Griffin testified infringed on individual rights and were discriminatory. A third bill, her own proposal, would have given her office sweeping access to all medical records in the state, which are now protected by medical privacy laws.

Governor Landry did not publicly push for the measures, a sign that they may not be priorities for his administration. A majority of Louisiana voters support school vaccine mandates, according to polls by Louisiana Families for Vaccines and the Center for Individual Freedom. Most proposals to weaken vaccine laws also failed in other states this year.

Since her appointment, Dr. Griffin has traveled the state to meet with residents. In June, she and her husband wandered through a wellness event, sponsored by the Northshore Alternative Health Alliance, in Mandeville. She had been invited to give the keynote address by Abigail Licatino, a member of Health Freedom Louisiana who has said that vaccines cause “most” autism.

Booths featured local farmers, reiki practitioners, functional medicine doctors, chiropractors, spiritual healers and purveyors of peptides, supplements and IV treatments. The event represented some of the “holistic approaches” Dr. Griffin said she planned to highlight as surgeon general.

In speeches before her appointment, Dr. Griffin had offered a far-reaching vision. While conventional medicine would still play an indispensable role, she said, the current health system was failing Americans and would “collapse.” The health freedom and wellness movements would help show “the path forward.”

Kitty Bennett, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Murder Drops to Historic Lows in Baltimore
item.description:
Murder makes work.

A soon as somebody is killed, an enormous machinery kicks into gear, driven by cops and medics, nurses and lawyers, ministers and morticians. The mechanics aren’t that different city to city, but in Baltimore the machinery has been as active and infamous as anywhere.

Now it is operating in a Baltimore that no one alive has experienced and few could have imagined. So far in 2026, Baltimore has recorded fewer homicides than ever at this point of the year, an incredible milestone in a place once morbidly referred to as “Bodymore.”

For most of the past 50 years, the city’s annual murder total exceeded 200. It ran above 300 for most of the last decade — a multiyear eruption of violence after the 2015 death of Freddie Gray from injuries in police custody. This year, the police commissioner aims for the count to stay under 100. It isn’t unattainable. From January to August, there were 60 murders. There were 45 in July 2015 alone.

Across the country, homicides have fallen to record lows after a surge during the pandemic years. But the steepness of the decline in Baltimore stands out even against that backdrop.

What happened? Violent crime rates rise and fall for countless reasons: some enigmatic mix of policy, practice, economics and other unknowable factors. Credit or blame are impossible to assign precisely, though not for lack of trying.

Just down Interstate 95 in Washington, no less a figure than President Trump is claiming credit for a drop in crime in the capital that was well underway before he returned to office. Last summer, he sent thousands of troops and federal officers into a city he declared was overrun with “bloodshed, bedlam and squalor.”

The effects of what the White House calls the “unrelenting” efforts of Mr. Trump’s D.C. task force and the thousands of arrests it has made will be long debated. But the drop in crime in Baltimore has been almost entirely on the city’s own terms. The overall number of arrests in the city is far below what it was a dozen years ago. It would have been unimaginable in the raw aftermath of Mr. Gray’s death, when a scathing civil rights investigation into Baltimore’s police department, released a decade ago this month, found the force was overly aggressive and ineffective.

The mayor has championed an array of programs to defuse tensions in volatile neighborhoods, enlisting those who know the fundamentals of street violence firsthand. Baltimore’s top prosecutor has focused on making illegally carrying guns, let alone using them, a very risky proposition in a city rife with firearms.

There is still plenty of violence in the city. Shootings remain routine. Murder is not a rarity. The machine still has work.

But the difference is real: At this point four years ago, nearly 160 more people had been killed in Baltimore.

For those who were on duty when the bloodshed was at its worst, this new reality has been almost hard to fathom. And in a scarred city, they only hope it can last.

“There’d be no way I’d be doing this right now,” said Detective Jonathan L. “J.J.” Jones, who has worked in the Baltimore police’s homicide unit for nearly two decades.

Detective Jones, 49, was rolling through Westport, a neighborhood in south Baltimore, looking for someone among the rowhouses. The case was all but closed; a suspect had confessed. But he thought the evidence could be “tightened.”

“I can play the long game now,” he said.

In the 2010s and early 2020s, when bodies lined the hallway at the medical examiner’s office, Detective Jones would be handed three new murder cases in a week, nearly as many as policing experts say detectives should be given in a year. He would come into work on a Wednesday and not return home until Sunday, rotating through changes of clothes he kept at the office.

That there are simply fewer murders to investigate is a big reason Baltimore’s homicide clearance rate — the share of cases that result in an arrest — has risen to 60 percent this year, significantly above the national average, from 31 percent in 2015.

Historically, many of the city’s murders have come out of disputes between small gangs or drug crews, bloody attempts to settle scores or send messages. This was the kind of violence portrayed on “The Wire,” the show that gave epic dimension to the struggle over the streets of Baltimore.

These days, Detective Jones said, fewer of the victims seem to be targets, more of them casualties of reckless gunfire. Some of the veteran drug dealers, men proficient at the use of violence, have been locked up, he said. The suspects now are more careless, less streetwise. It’s easier to get them to talk.

It is not a good idea to say all of this out loud, Detective Jones said, wary of jinxing things. He is genuinely nervous that the progress may be more fragile than people realize.

“It’s really weird now,” he said. “You have these young detectives saying there’s nothing going on.”

He tells them to shut up.

“It won’t always be like this.”

For now, his blood pressure is down and he spends more time with his family, including his 19-year-old son. Detective Jones recalled cases he’d worked on with victims that age. Houses and street corners all along his drive through the city recalled past killings.

“These are the things I can think about now,” he said. “Before I was just running. The more time you have to sit and think about stuff, the more it gets to you.”

At the sound of four chimes — the signal from “the box” — the nurses in the R. Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center at the University of Maryland Medical Center prepared for a new visitor. A young man with a gunshot wound was wheeled in on a gurney. “Embarrassing,” he muttered. He had accidentally shot himself in the armpit.

The trauma ward is the primary destination for people on the worst days of their lives. Patients are brought by ambulance, flown in by helicopter and in some cases dropped off on the front sidewalk. Freddie Gray spent his last days there in a coma.

Any minute, some major calamity can turn the ward into a whirlwind of activity. This has always been true. But something has changed about the gun violence cases.

“It’s still happening, it’s just not as severe,” said CJ Meyer, 53, a senior clinical nurse who left a job at a law office for the more unforgiving demands of emergency medicine.

Several years ago, she said, people would come in with multiple gunshot wounds. Now, “they’re getting shot in the arm or shot in the leg,” she said. “They’re not dying.” And gunfire accounts for even fewer of those brought to the trauma ward by violence.

Of the 929 violent injury patients admitted in fiscal year 2023, roughly half had been shot. The rest had been stabbed or otherwise assaulted. This past year, there were 159 fewer patients, and the share with gunshot wounds had fallen to a third.

This may be due partly to the prosecutor’s crackdown on illegal gun possession. Ms. Meyer is not in a position to theorize. “We never know the stories,” she said.

The medical staff’s job is only to keep people alive. These days, that often means seeing people with bullet and knife injuries through surgery and rehab, making the stays for these patients longer than they used to be. But they are less likely to end with a somber notification in the family room.

Michael Dunty started his job at the Baltimore prosecutor’s office right after Freddie Gray’s death. When he joined the homicide unit a year later, “I was handed, I don’t know, maybe 10 or 12 charged homicide cases that were pending in court.”

As dozens of prosecutors quit under the then-state’s attorney Marilyn Mosby and trials were delayed by the pandemic, the caseload compounded. In 2022, a typical prosecutor in the unit had more than two dozen homicide cases on the court schedule, Mr. Dunty said. One handled 17 homicide jury trials in a single year. And the murders did not stop: Beyond the cases in court, each prosecutor was working on 20 to 25 open investigations.

“We all recognized it wasn’t sustainable,” said Mr. Dunty, 51, now chief of the homicide division.

Ivan J. Bates became state’s attorney in 2023, promising to hire more people and aggressively prosecute gun crimes. Since then, more than 1,500 people charged with illegal gun possession, mostly because of prior violent felonies, have been sent to prison.

In Mr. Dunty’s division, prosecutors are now handling around a dozen charged cases and, in the most stunning change, only four or five open murder investigations.

“We’re still seeing the same kind of types of homicides that we were over the years,” Mr. Dunty said, referring to drug deals and beefs. “We’re just seeing less of them.”

In certain neighborhoods, generations knew the name Dennis Wise, even though he’d be absent from the city for nearly 40 years. Convicted of murder in 1979 — prosecutors described him as a hit man — Mr. Wise was a living urban legend. A character based on him in “The Wire” is simply named Dennis Wise.

When he was released in 2017, Mr. Wise returned to a different Baltimore. The guns were deadlier and everyone seemed to have one. Gangs from the West Coast had arrived. After the Freddie Gray protests, he said, “police were standing back and letting people kill each other.”

But he was intrigued by a mentorship program called Safe Streets, which he’d learned about from a man he’d known in prison.

There are many elements to Mayor Brandon Scott’s violence prevention plan, but most attention has focused on the Group Violence Reduction Strategy. This is based on the concept that a small group of people drive most of the violence. In weekly meetings at a Baltimore church, police officers, city employees and members of community organizations discuss people they have reason to believe are likely to be perpetrators or victims of violent crime. Members of the group visit these people, warning that the they are on the city’s radar but also offering services, including housing assistance and job training.

Variations of the approach have been tried in other cities and twice before in Baltimore, with mixed results. But criminologists studying the current iteration found that in the police district where it was initially put into place, violence dropped measurably.

There are other pieces to the mayor’s plan, including intervention teamslike Safe Streets, which has operated in Baltimore since 2007. Some of these programs rely on “credible messengers,” a jargony way of saying people with a background on the streets.

Mr. Wise joined Safe Streets soon after his release. He worked out of a school building, talking to young people on the corners and mediating disputes. People listened to him, said Mr. Wise, now 75 and soft-spoken, “because they know I’ve been through a lot of things.”

Mr. Wise’s background gives him authority, but histories like his also bring the program risk. In June, a 51-year-old Safe Streets worker who had spent 10 years in prison was arrested on a federal gun charge.

To the critics of the program, Mr. Wise counters: Who else would have the trust of a young man with a gun and a grudge? “When I was I was coming up, in order to be safe, you had to be known to be dangerous,” he said. He insisted the numbers showed that was changing.

“When you stop being people getting shot, you know you’re making progress,” he said.

Albert P. Wylie opened his first funeral home in 1993, when homicides hit a record high. This was the era when his son, Brandon, was learning the trade.

He learned that the funerals of murder victims were often paid for by the local drug dealer. He learned that families appreciated little celebratory items, like wristbands, when the person being mourned had not made it out of his teens.

“Not a lot to celebrate,” the younger Mr. Wylie said. “Obituaries were short.”

Young people have a lot more to do these days, he said. There are classes and community groups in places where there used to be nothing but the corner. Social media can be a problem, with videos of shootings and carjackings going viral. But, he said, the phone has also diluted the sway of the local street crews.

“It’s not so much about your corner anymore,” he said. “It’s decentralized.”

There seem to be more people dying by suicide these days, Mr. Wylie said. And there are still killings, even if they are fewer. The funeral home held recently services for three victims, he said. But he was optimistic. “I have hope for the city,” he said.

And as mourners gathered in the lobby after a midday service, Mr. Wylie pointed out that murder wasn’t the only fact of life and death in Baltimore.

“No I can’t say that we’re as busy with homicides,” he said. “But I’m busy. I’m always busy.”

item.title: What Do Students Lose When They Stop Writing?
item.description:
After years of studying how human beings write, the cognitive psychologist Ronald T. Kellogg concluded that drafting a basic persuasive essay was as mentally taxing as digging a ditch was physically exhausting.

Writing well requires a command of vocabulary, spelling and grammar. It forces writers to comprehend a subject, to sift through their working memory of that topic, to organize and plan. Writing an essay is so difficult that a person in the throes of it can do hardly anything else — as anyone who has shushed a spouse or child while trying to compose a decent sentence can attest.

Very few people would volunteer to dig a ditch. Likewise, it is hard — almost impossible, many English teachers will admit — to turn a reluctant writer into an enthusiastic one.

Yet the American education system expects nearly all students to learn how to write an essay. It’s little wonder, then, that as soon as a tool arrived promising to lessen the pain people grabbed it.

Like it or not, artificial intelligence is now firmly embedded in how students produce text. Somewhere between two-thirds and 90 percent of high school and college students are already using A.I. for schoolwork, according to recent surveys, often requesting help with writing assignments.

A growing number of educators are alarmed, and insist that students should write without A.I. These teachers are returning to handwriting, blue books and proctored, in-class essay tests — all attempts to prevent students from outsourcing their writing to chatbots.

This is baffling to tech industry leaders, who see A.I. rejection as a form of educational malpractice. They point out that writing is already the leading use of A.I. in the workplace, and argue there is no need to continue suffering through the task without help. After all, they say, chatbots now exceed the ability of most human beings to produce fluent prose.

All this points to some questions about writing itself: Why work so hard to learn it? And what do students stand to lose when they stop facing down a blank page, alone with their thoughts?

The scholars who study writing and cognition are rarely reflexively opposed to A.I. Many have spent decades anticipating a leap in computer-assisted writing, just like the one we are living through. They tend to be excited by the technology’s potential.

Still, their work casts doubt on the tech-industry push to embed A.I. at every stage of the student writing process, from brainstorming to drafting to revising. Research shows that traditional, unassisted composition is valuable, not despite its difficulty, but because of it. Writing builds our working memory, executive planning skills and metacognition — the ability to think about our thinking, weigh alternate viewpoints and revise for clarity and style. It takes decades to develop writing skills, from toddlerhood into adulthood.

“Writing is a technology for thinking,” Dr. Kellogg said.

Learning to write did not always matter so much.

Before the 1870s, American students were tested through oral exams. College seats were reserved for the elite — future ministers and lawyers, professions where public speaking dominated.

But the rise of the modern, urban economy, and the invention of the typewriter, produced jobs that dealt more heavily with the written word, like office clerks and advertising copywriters. Starting in the late 19th century, students needed to learn how to write more fluently, and school curriculums, tied closely to the demands of industry, adapted. As more students went to college, and class sizes grew, administering oral tests also became too time-consuming, according to the linguist Naomi S. Baron, who traces this history in her book “Who Wrote This?”

Besides, teachers discovered that writing itself deepened knowledge. “If you want to think, understand and learn something, text really is preferable,” Dr. Baron said.

Cognitive research confirms that writing is a powerful aid in helping us to retain information we read. The work of writing forces us to stress-test our ideas, allowing the writer to respond to counterarguments and cite sources. Revision is a practice of self-critique and self-improvement, and can be social, as well, if feedback is elicited. Writing can also be empowering, allowing us to share our experiences and express our views. It can even be healing, which is why therapists sometimes suggest keeping a journal.

It is not clear if these benefits can be fully realized when writing alongside artificial intelligence. There are reasons to be wary.

Last year, a small study from M.I.T. showed that individuals who wrote in partnership with A.I. chatbots recorded lower brain activity while they wrote, compared with those who worked without chatbots. The writers who used A.I. struggled to remember what, exactly, they had written, and felt little ownership over their work.

The findings join a growing body of research suggesting that frequent A.I. use can degrade critical thinking.

Nevertheless, tech companies are aggressively marketing A.I. writing assistants to students and schools.

Jenny Maxwell, general manager for education at Superhuman, the A.I. company that makes the popular writing app Grammarly, told me that we are living through a “burn it down” moment for teaching and learning. Educators who try to withhold A.I. writing tools are essentially announcing to their students — “consumers,” she called them — that their coursework is irrelevant to the job market.

She did acknowledge that some basic, human writing skills remain valuable. Students need to write well enough to have a sense of which A.I. text suggestions to accept and which to reject, she said. Ms. Maxwell also insisted that creativity in writing would persist, because people would still want to express their personal voice and style.

To that end, companies like Grammarly, Google and OpenAI are creating so-called Socratic versions of their chatbots, sold to schools as writing helpers that will guide students through assignments without doing the work for them.

I tested Gemini Guided Learning, from Google, and ChatGPT Study Mode, from OpenAI, feeding each a standard freshman composition assignment that requires students to write about a childhood reading experience that shaped them. I began by telling the chatbots that my mother had gifted me a beautiful, illustrated hardcover of “Anne of Green Gables.”

At first, the Socratic chatbots behaved as I expected, asking questions: Where did you grow up? Did you read the book curled up in your bedroom, or outside under a tree? Why did you relate to Anne as a character? It began to feel like a therapy session.

But eventually, each A.I. began to work independently, creating detailed outlines for my essay. These study buddies demurred when directed to “write the essay for me.” But when prompted to provide “an example of what these paragraphs could look like,” they spat out hundreds of polished, neatly structured words, in seconds. They quoted, often accurately, from literature.

A spokeswoman for Google said the company was working to develop a version of Guided Learning for schools, which would provide “stricter instructions to the system to ensure it guides students without doing the work for them.”

And in a written statement, Leah Belsky, vice president of education at OpenAI, said Study Mode “is an early and evolving set of experiences, and continued feedback from educators and students will shape how we approach learning, safety, privacy and academic integrity.”

(The New York Times is suing OpenAI, along with two other companies, Microsoft and Perplexity, for copyright infringement.)

A.I. is already ubiquitous: on every device, in every web search, insisting that it can summarize for us, analyze for us, write for us. It steps in even when we have not invited it.

For students with still-developing minds, the most urgent question, then, is how to protect thinking in a world where it has become so easy to outsource writing.

We might begin by considering what A.I. is actually good at when it comes to composition. A.I. can be especially useful for those with disabilities or who are nonnative English speakers, said Steve Graham, a writing expert and educational psychologist at Arizona State University. Chatbots can correct grammar and suggest potential trims or revisions for clarity. With A.I., there have been immense strides in accurate voice-to-text transcription for writers who cannot physically type or write by hand.

And A.I. can offer all of this help privately, with no need to be vulnerable and expose a rough first draft to another person’s judgment. For many American students, especially the third with below-basic literacy skills, the writing process can be painful and embarrassing, and a reason many dread homework and exams.

But, Dr. Graham cautioned, there is no part of the writing process that can be handed over to A.I. without some cost. Intellectual growth occurs at every stage, from brainstorming to fine-tuning a final draft. If writing is thinking, then any part of the struggle that is outsourced to technology amounts to relinquishing some freedom to perceive. How will students ever know what they really think of anything — whether it’s “The Crucible” or A.I. itself — if they ask a machine to spit out an answer for them?

Last year, a group of writing experts, including Dr. Graham, assembled at the University of California, Irvine, to produce recommendations to schools.

They did not reject A.I. Instead, they called on schools to resist the temptation to devote less time to writing — not because it will continue to be such a critical skill in the workplace, where it’s already waning, but to sharpen the mind.

Writing should be embedded across the curriculum, they advised. Students should continue to do the hard work of drafting their own sentences, paragraphs and eventually full essays about their lives and about what they have read, both fiction and nonfiction. All this teaches grammar and vocabulary, certainly. But it also allows students to master the knowledge they are gaining.

There is room for A.I., these experts suggested: The technology can help educators generate engaging writing prompts on whatever subjects they are teaching.

Teachers might also encourage students to use A.I. to get initial feedback on their writing before turning it in. Anna Mills, a writing instructor at the College of Marin in California, has developed detailed A.I. prompts that students can use to elicit useful feedback without outsourcing all the work.

Still, there is probably a need to limit access to the technology.

The University of Sydney has developed a policy known as the two-lane approach. Across every discipline, professors are required to give some assessments in person under secure conditions, limiting A.I. use. But they must also allow A.I. for other assessments, so students can show they know how to apply the technology.

This spring I visited John Jay High School, in the New York suburbs, to report on how one English teacher, Jessica Binney, was dealing with A.I.

In a creative-writing class, she had students prompt a chatbot to write a poem. The results were predictably generic, so students then asked the chatbot to make revisions, considering where the bot performed well and where it fell short.

Still, like many educators, she had tired of policing A.I. misuse on take-home assignments. In her Advanced Placement English course, she moved much of the essay writing, produced inside the classroom, to pen and paper.

For the most part, students did not complain. Many had already been through an initial whirlwind romance with A.I., before rethinking their relationship with the tools. Ainsley Graham, a junior, told me she was thrilled by ChatGPT’s ability to help with data analysis in a science research class, but recognized the risks of using chatbots to write essays about literature.

“You’re not strengthening that muscle by actually analyzing these really hard texts,” she said. “They’re meant to be hard.”

When Cassady Tondorf, 17, learned how chatbots produced writing, she realized their utter lack of originality. “The entire internet is open to it,” she said. “It’s just regenerating the same things, over and over.”

If she wanted to be valuable on the job market, she felt, she would need to have ideas and skills that were uniquely her own.

item.title: Democratic Socialists Look for Upsets in Hostile Territory: Florida
item.description:
Florida does not jump off the electoral map as fertile territory for democratic socialists. President Trump won the state, which has shifted right in recent years, by 13 percentage points in 2024. And in many Latin American communities in South Florida, socialism is a dirty word.

Yet three underdog democratic socialist candidates are trying to prove that the way for the Democratic Party to regain relevance in a state that not long ago was the nation’s premier political battleground is by embracing the left, not recoiling from it.

They are running in primaries for the House and the Senate on Tuesday on a message of change, championing “Medicare for All,” rent stabilization and abolishing ICE. Their campaigns, which have stoked tensions inside the Democratic Party, offer a fresh test of the bounds of a left-wing movement that has built some momentum in a primary season where they have had mixed results.

“It does not have to be this way,” State Representative Angie Nixon of Jacksonville, a progressive firebrand who is seeking the Democratic nomination for Senate, said at a campaign event on Friday night that drew a mostly young crowd. “We deserve the opportunity to be healthy, to be prosperous, to be safe, to experience joy.”

Ms. Nixon made her comments at a joint rally in Fort Lauderdale with two House candidates, Oliver Larkin and Elijah Manley, and Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan.

The event divided Florida Democrats. Organizers changed venues after a State Representative Michael Gottlieb, a Democrat who is the chairman of the Florida Legislative Jewish Caucus, objected to the inclusion of Ms. Tlaib, an outspoken critic of the Israeli government. Mr. Gottlieb also expressed concern that the rally was supporting people who are running against Jewish candidates.

A win by any of the three candidates would be considered a major upset. Ms. Nixon, 42, a three-term state lawmaker, is running against Alex Vindman, a top witness in Mr. Trump’s first impeachment trial, who has far outraised her in the Democratic Senate race.

Mr. Larkin, 34, is challenging Representative Jared Moskowitz, after Republican state lawmakers redrew the congressional map and eliminated Mr. Moskowitz’s old district. Mr. Manley, 27, is one of several candidates running against Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, a former Democratic National Committee chairwoman. Her old seat was also eliminated, and she is now running in a historically Black district.

The front-runners have engaged little, if at all, with their left-wing challengers.

“Do I think that Broward County Democrats are moving towards embracing the fringe left?” Ms. Wasserman Schultz asked The South Florida Sun Sentinel. “No, firmly no.”

Mr. Larkin has been a democratic socialist since 2020. Ms. Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America this year, though she has downplayed that affiliation. Mr. Manley is not a member of the organization but campaigns with it and said he identifies as a democratic socialist.

That any strain of progressivism is alive in Florida might surprise even some Floridians. Since taking office, Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, turned the state into a laboratory for right-wing policy that was at the forefront of the national culture wars.

But during that time, Florida has also gotten more expensive. Wealthier people have moved to the state, driving up home prices and pushing out working-age residents who can no longer afford the cost of living, especially in big cities such as Miami and Orlando.

“We are not a conservative state,” Richie Floyd, the vice chairman of the City Council in St. Petersburg, Fla., said at the rally. In 2021, he became the first democratic socialist elected to office in what appeared to be more than a century. “We are not a right-wing state, he said. “We are a working-class state.”

Since Mr. Trump first won Florida in 2016, the state has elected Republicans to many offices while also approving liberal ballot measures restoring felons’ voting rights, raising the minimum wage and legalizing medical marijuana. Those outcomes have led Florida Democrats to believe that liberal policies can win favor even if their party’s brand has struggled.

But to run as any kind of socialist is especially difficult in South Florida, which has been shaped by the politics of Cuban exiles who fled the island’s 1959 Communist revolution. Other Latin American immigrants, including from Colombia, Venezuela and Nicaragua, also settled in the area after fleeing left-wing governments or violence.

Progressives say they have been buoyed by the success of left-wing and progressive candidates across the country, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and democratic socialists who have ousted House incumbents. And they have tried to make a Florida-specific argument, pointing to a progressive candidate for governor who came close to winning in 2018, during Mr. Trump’s first midterm.

Centrist Democrats in Florida have rolled their eyes at progressives’ contention, countering that a more moderate candidate could have defeated Mr. DeSantis in 2018.

Democrats have since tended to follow the centrist line and failed to recapture the state’s most powerful offices. The party front-runners this year follow that trend with Mr. Vindman, a retired Army lieutenant colonel, in the Senate race, and David Jolly, a former Republican congressman, in the governor’s race.

“I’m a former Republican,” Mr. Jolly recently told MS NOW. “I spent five years as an independent.”

Progressives argue they have invested in field organizing and social media in a way that their more moderate counterparts have not. Two social media creators canvassed for Ms. Nixon in the suburban Broward County city of Miramar in stifling heat on Friday afternoon.

Few voters answered the door. Of those who did, only one mentioned Mr. Vindman. A few others said they knew of Ms. Nixon.

Lorraine Shim, 57, said she planned to vote on Election Day but would not say for whom. She said that no other campaign had knocked on her door yet this cycle.

“You’re the first,” she told the canvassers.
